extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and publishers interested in historical English copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal principles governing Crown (prerogative) copies, the King's printers, the Stationers' Company, and statutory deposit/registration requirements under the early English copyright statutes (e.g., Stat. 8 Anne and later acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's exclusive right of first publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Until the act of publication is accomplished, an author has an undoubted right to have full control over it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author may, by conduct, be taken to abandon his work and give the public power to publish it before the usual time of copyright has transpired, but there is little authority on when conduct effects such abandonment; example: delivering a manuscript to a bookseller with words like 'I will make a present of this work to you to publish.' (cases and authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative copyright in Crown (prerogative) copies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is said that the King by a prerogative right vested in the crown has the exclusive privilege of printing: (1) Acts of Parliament, Proclamations, Orders of Council, &c.; (2) The Liturgies and Books of Divine Service, &c.; and (3) The Bible. These works are called prerogative copies and patents have been granted to printers giving full power to print and re-print them to the exclusion of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence, extent and legal foundation of such a prerogative have been much questioned; some patents have been adjudged invalid when fully examined in common law courts. The text contrasts authorities and arguments on both sides and cites cases (e.g., Baskett v. University of Cambridge, Donaldson v. Becket).

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of long exercise (antiquity) as evidentiary but non-conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that long exercise of a prerogative right (since introduction of printing) supports its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument: length of time warrants no wrong; prerogative, as first assumed, may have been continually diminished. Historical exercise does not conclusively create a legal prerogative (cases and commentary cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/political convenience justification for limited exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If no general common law prerogative exists, it is said for political and public convenience the King, as supreme executive Magistrate, ought to promulgate acts of state and therefore may have an exclusive privilege of printing them at his own press or grantees'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterpoint: principle at its farthest extent only warrants printing a sufficient number for official use (judges, magistrates); afterwards any person may multiply copies for private convenience or profit. When the reason for the exclusive requirement ceases, the exclusivity ceases.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as Head of the Church: limited prerogative for liturgies
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that the King, as Head of the Church, has a right to publication of liturgies and books of divine service, and hence his patentee has exclusive privilege of printing forms of prayers for particular occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument: should be limited like the executive case — supply clergy and those concerned, but not to prevent subjects from making copies for themselves or printing for sale generally; the reason for the law determines its extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative by purchase/compilation at Crown expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly maintained that the King had rights by purchase to works compiled at the expense of the crown (e.g., law publications, Latin grammar) and therefore a prerogative copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-argument: purchases made with public money (government expense) cannot create private property of the King; purchase does not confer perpetual copyright akin to authorship; precedent and reasoning cited (cases and Lord Mansfield's observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on injunctions (Chancery) is not conclusive of legal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of crown copies is sometimes supported by injunctions granted in Chancery and by decisions in common law courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But injunctions may be granted for many reasons other than legality of the patent (e.g., to preserve status quo until trial), frequently temporary, and not conclusive on a court of common law. The change of chancery practice (granting injunctions until trial) weakens their value as proof of legal right; authorities and examples cited (cases where injunctions were granted then patent invalidated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common law copyright vs statute (perpetuity question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether an author at common law had a perpetual right to print and publish his work; Donaldson v. Becket created doubt over the existence of a perpetual common law copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the King or others claimed rights unaffected by Statute of Anne on account of common law/perpetual rights, that raises complex questions; the text canvasses judges' divided opinions and implications for crown prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to publish translations, abstracts, or editions with notes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is asserted that any one is at liberty to print Acts of Parliament and the Bible with notes, or to publish a translation/abstract from original texts and enjoy copyright in that new production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This point challenges a prerogative that would prevent annotated or derivative editions; Lord Mansfield admitted an abstract of court records might be published. The prerogative's claimed purpose (prevent mutilation/incorrect printing) does not clearly justify excluding annotated or translated editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory entry of title at Stationers' Hall (registration requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stat. 8 Anne and later acts provide that no person shall be subjected to penalties for printing or reprinting any book unless the title to the copy be entered in the register book of the Company of Stationers; entry within one calendar month of publication in London, within three months elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalty for failure: five pounds and the price of eleven copies, recoverable by managers of public libraries; later acts clarified that failure to enter does not affect copyright but only subjects publisher to penalty; fee for entry two shillings; register consult/certificate one shilling; if clerk refuses entry an advertisement in the Gazette has equivalent benefits and clerk forfeits twenty pounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry of assignee's consent required to bind assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is not answerable to the assignee unless the consent of the proprietor, by which he parted with the copyright, is entered in the register in like manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence assignments should be recorded in the Stationers' register to be effective against purchasers/assignees (statutory direction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration rules for periodicals and first numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In making entries at Stationers' Hall of magazines, reviews, or other periodical publications, it is sufficient to make the entry within one month next after the publication of the first number or volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows a single initial entry to cover serial publications (statutory provision cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory deposit (delivery) of copies to public libraries and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute required delivery of copies of each book to certain public libraries: originally nine copies, later eleven copies (including British Museum, Bodleian, Cambridge, Trinity College Dublin, King's Inn Dublin, Scottish universities, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery: publisher to deliver eleven copies of the largest impression with maps/prints on demand in writing within one twelve months of publication, to the warehouse-keeper for use of specified libraries; warehouse-keeper to deliver within one month to keepers of libraries; penalties for non-delivery (five pounds plus value) and for neglect by warehouseman; second editions not to be delivered unless they contain additions/alterations (or additions delivered separately). Warehouse-keeper to transmit lists quarterly to librarians and to call for demanded copies; publisher may deliver directly in which case receipt by librarian is equivalent.
